name: German states before unification
summary: The many kingdoms, duchies and free cities of Germany, such as Bavaria, Saxony, Hanover and Württemberg. Members of the Holy Roman Empire until 1806, they joined the German Confederation (1815–66) and then the German Empire (1871).

location.value: Central Europe; the Confederation had 39 predominantly German-speaking sovereign states (34 at its dissolution in 1866).

terrain.value: Plains in the north, uplands in the middle, and the Alps in the south.

climate.value: Temperate, with cold winters and mild summers.

resources.value: Farmland, forests, Saxon silver and coal.

disasters.value: Hunger years after the 1815 volcanic eruption (1816–17) and potato blight (1846–47).

population.value: The article gives the population excluding Austria as about 21 million in 1815, rising to about 34 million in 1865. No figure of 30 million is given.

urbanisation.value: Munich, Dresden, Hamburg, Frankfurt and Cologne were the main cities.

disease.value: Cholera struck in 1831–32 and again in later epidemics.

economicBase.value: Farm output rose after 1815. The Zollverein customs union began in 1834 and covered most states by 1842. Outside Prussia, industry grew slowly.

tradeRoutes.value: The Rhine and Elbe rivers and the Hanseatic cities such as Hamburg and Bremen carried goods.

wealth.value: Wealth varied by state, with industrial Saxony and the Rhineland richer than the rural east.

moneyAndTax.value: Many currencies circulated, including the gulden and thaler.

inequality.value: A wide gap between nobles and peasants, easing after the reforms of the early 1800s.

governmentType.value: A loose confederation of monarchies and four free cities: Bremen, Frankfurt, Hamburg and Lübeck.

keyRulers.value: Ludwig II of Bavaria asked Wilhelm to take the imperial crown; Hanover was ruled by the British king until 1837. Ludwig I and the Saxon kings are not named on the page.

succession.value: Most states were ruled by hereditary dynasties.

institutions.value: The Federal Diet in Frankfurt (1815–66) united the states loosely.

stability.value: The Revolutions of 1848 challenged the princes and called for a united Germany.

eliteConflict.value: Austria and Prussia competed for leadership.

armyAndTech.value: Small state armies, with Prussia and Austria the main military powers.

majorWars.value: The Austro-Prussian War (1866) ended the Confederation.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: German Confederation (checked 12 Nov 2026); Britannica: German Confederation (checked 15 Nov 2026) (the Zollverein (1834) and the revolutions of 1848 weakened it; the Seven Weeks’ War of 1866 ended it)

territoryChange.value: Hundreds of states merged into about 39 (1803–15).

alliancesRivals.value: Caught between Austria and Prussia, which competed for leadership.

inventions.value: Printing in many towns; early railways (1835).

openness.value: Trade opened up across the states after the Zollverein customs union (1834).

communicationTransport.value: Railways began in 1835 and spread quickly after 1840.

religion.value: The infobox lists Catholic and Protestant; the page does not describe a south–north split.

artsArchitecture.value: Music by Bach, Beethoven and others, Romantic poetry and painting, and many Baroque palaces.

sharedIdentity.value: Shared language and culture before a nation-state.

dailyLife.value: Most people lived in villages or small capital towns, eating bread, potatoes and sausage.

neighbours.value: France, Austria, Prussia, Denmark, Netherlands, Switzerland.

colonisation.value: None; the German states had no overseas colonies before 1871.

riseSignals.value: Established by the Ninth Act of the Congress of Vienna on 8 June 1815. The Peace of Westphalia is not mentioned in the article.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: German Confederation (checked 12 Nov 2026); Britannica: German Confederation (checked 15 Nov 2026) (39 states, set up by the Congress of Vienna in 1815; the Peace of Westphalia is not mentioned and the article gives 9 June 1815 for the treaty date)

peakPeriod.value: The page does not mention a cultural golden age.

declineSignals.value: Prussia won the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 and went on to unify Germany in 1871.

outcome.value: Dissolved after the Austro-Prussian War; the Peace of Prague (23 August 1866) recognised its dissolution. The German Empire was proclaimed in 1871 (the article gives 1 or 18 January).
outcome.source: Wikipedia: German Confederation (checked 12 Nov 2026); Britannica: German Confederation (checked 15 Nov 2026) (dissolved after Prussia beat Austria in 1866, leading to the North German Confederation; the Peace of Prague and 1871 are not in the article)

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
